## For the staff

- Pushing the ball after the opponent scores is a **style choice that neither costs nor wins
  much**. In close games, playing a second faster than your usual pace goes with slightly
  better possessions, but the gain is small and uncertain.
- A naive look says the opposite (pushing hurts). That is likely, at least in part, the
  **score talking**: teams that are behind speed up, so the bad nights are also the fast ones.
- What separates teams is **what they do with these possessions**, not how fast they start
  them. Every live-ball turnover hands the opponent a possession worth about 0.2 points more
  than a made basket does.
:::

# The question

After the opponent scores, a team can inbound and attack before the defense is set, or walk the
ball up and run its half-court offense. Does pushing pay, once the cost of turnovers is counted,
and does it pay more for some teams than for others?

Every possession after an opponent's made field goal is measured by **the seconds of game clock
until its first action** (shot, shooting foul or turnover; the inbound is included, because
inbounding quickly is part of pushing) and by its **net points**: points scored minus the
league-average value of the possession it hands to the opponent. A steal hands the opponent
`r fmt(read_rds(here("data", "processed", "next_possession_values.rds")) %>% filter(start_type == "Off Steal") %>% pull(value) %>% mean(), 2)`
points per possession; a made basket,
`r fmt(read_rds(here("data", "processed", "next_possession_values.rds")) %>% filter(grepl("Make", start_type), start_type != "Off FT Make") %>% pull(value) %>% mean(), 2)`.

# What the data show

## Strict fast breaks are rare after a made basket

```{r}
#| label: fig-delta
#| fig-cap: "Seconds of game clock from the opponent's made field goal to the first action. The dashed line is the FIBA fast-break limit (8 s)."
#| fig-height: 4
analysed %>%
  filter(delta_s <= 30) %>%
  ggplot(aes(delta_s)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, boundary = -0.5, fill = "grey70", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 8.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = accent) +
  annotate("text", x = 8.8, y = Inf, vjust = 1.5, hjust = 0, size = 3.5, colour = accent,
           label = paste0("Fast break (FIBA): ", scales::percent(share_fast_break, 1),
                          " of possessions")) +
  facet_wrap(~season) +
  labs(x = "Seconds to first action after the opponent scores", y = "Possessions") +
  theme_report()
```

Only `r scales::percent(share_fast_break, 1)` of these possessions are fast breaks in the FIBA
sense. Pushing after a make usually ends in early offense, so intention is measured as a
continuous pace, not as a count of fast breaks.

## Teams have a pace identity after makes

```{r}
#| label: fig-team-pace
#| fig-cap: "Average seconds to first action after the opponent scores, by team-season. Colour: overall pace (possessions per game, all situations)."
#| fig-height: 7
team_games %>%
  group_by(season, team) %>%
  summarise(pace_after_makes = weighted.mean(mean_delta, n_poss), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(pace, by = c("season", "team")) %>%
  mutate(label = reorder(paste(team, season), -pace_after_makes)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(pace_after_makes, label, colour = poss_per_game)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "plasma", end = 0.9, name = "Possessions per game") +
  facet_wrap(~season, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Seconds to first action after the opponent scores (lower = faster)", y = NULL) +
  theme_report(10)
```

Usual paces span about four seconds across team-seasons, from about
`r fmt(min(team_games %>% group_by(team_season) %>% summarise(x = weighted.mean(mean_delta, n_poss)) %>% pull(x)), 1)`
to `r fmt(max(team_games %>% group_by(team_season) %>% summarise(x = weighted.mean(mean_delta, n_poss)) %>% pull(x)), 1)`
seconds.
Teams that push after makes tend to play fast overall too, but not always.

## Teams stick to their pace from game to game

```{r}
#| label: fig-within-between
#| fig-cap: "Average seconds to first action in each game (dots) for eight team-seasons of 2024-25, from the fastest to the slowest. Diamonds: season average."
#| fig-height: 4.5
sel <- team_games %>%
  filter(season == "2024-25") %>%
  group_by(team_season) %>%
  summarise(avg = weighted.mean(mean_delta, n_poss)) %>%
  arrange(avg) %>%
  slice(round(seq(1, n(), length.out = 8)))
team_games %>%
  filter(team_season %in% sel$team_season) %>%
  mutate(team_season = factor(team_season, levels = rev(sel$team_season))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(mean_delta, team_season)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.15, alpha = 0.35, size = 1.2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(aes(avg, team_season), data = sel %>%
               mutate(team_season = factor(team_season, levels = rev(sel$team_season))),
             shape = 23, size = 3.5, fill = accent, colour = "white", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Average seconds to first action in the game", y = NULL) +
  theme_report()
```

Part of the game-to-game scatter is noise from averaging about 30 possessions. Once the model
separates it, a team's true pace moves about **`r fmt(hyper_value("all", "tau"), 2)` s** from
game to game, while usual paces differ across teams by about
**`r fmt(hyper_value("all", "sigma_m"), 2)` s**: roughly
`r scales::percent(hyper_value("all", "sigma_m")^2 / (hyper_value("all", "sigma_m")^2 + hyper_value("all", "tau")^2), 1)`
of the variation in a game's pace is who the team is.

## The score moves the pace

```{r}
#| label: fig-score
#| fig-cap: "Average seconds to first action by score margin when the possession starts (offense's point of view)."
#| fig-height: 3.8
analysed %>%
  mutate(margin = cut(start_margin, c(-Inf, -10, -5, -1, 0, 4, 9, Inf),
                      labels = c("Down 10+", "Down 5-9", "Down 1-4", "Tied",
                                 "Up 1-4", "Up 5-9", "Up 10+"))) %>%
  group_by(margin) %>%
  summarise(delta = mean(delta_s), se = sd(delta_s) / sqrt(n())) %>%
  ggplot(aes(margin, delta)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = delta - 2 * se, ymax = delta + 2 * se), colour = accent) +
  labs(x = "Score margin at the start of the possession", y = "Seconds to first action") +
  theme_report()
```

Teams behind push to catch up and teams ahead slow down. So a naive comparison mixes the choice
to push with the score. The model is therefore fitted three times: on all possessions, on
close games (quarters 1-3, within 5 points) and on first quarters, where the game starts tied.

# Does pushing pay?

The model compares each team **with itself**: in games where it plays faster than its own usual
pace after makes, are those possessions better or worse? That is the **return**, in net points
per 100 possessions per second faster.

```{r}
#| label: fig-three
#| fig-cap: "Mean return across the league and the between-team association, in the three analyses. Median and 90% interval."
#| fig-height: 3.6
hyper_table %>%
  filter(variable %in% c("beta_bar", "gamma")) %>%
  mutate(analysis = factor(analysis_labels[analysis], levels = rev(analysis_labels)),
         variable = recode(variable,
                           beta_bar = "Return: a team playing faster than its own habit",
                           gamma = "Between teams: habitually faster teams")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(median, analysis)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = grey_line) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = q5, xmax = q95), linewidth = 1.1, colour = accent) +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = accent) +
  facet_wrap(~variable) +
  labs(x = "Net points per 100 possessions after makes, per second faster", y = NULL) +
  theme_report()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-three
#| tbl-cap: "Mean return per second faster than the team's usual pace (net points per 100), with the posterior probability that it is positive."
tibble(analysis = names(analysis_labels)) %>%
  mutate(
    Analysis = analysis_labels[analysis],
    Possessions = analysis_detail[analysis],
    `Mean return (90% interval)` = map_chr(analysis, fmt_interval, variable = "beta_bar",
                                           digits = 2),
    `P(return > 0)` = map_chr(fits[analysis], prob_positive, variable = "beta_bar")
  ) %>%
  select(-analysis) %>%
  kable()
```

With all possessions, the return is slightly negative. In close games and first quarters, where
the score has little say, the sign flips to slightly positive, with intervals that still include
zero. Pushing does not hurt when the game is even; it may help a little.

## Is it different for some teams?

```{r}
#| label: fig-team-returns
#| fig-cap: "Return of each team-season in the three analyses (median and 80% interval). Intervals overlap almost completely."
#| fig-height: 11
imap_dfr(fits, return_table) %>%
  mutate(analysis = factor(analysis_labels[analysis], levels = analysis_labels),
         team_season = reorder(team_season, med)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(med, team_season, colour = analysis)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = grey_line) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), position = position_dodge(width = 0.7)) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), size = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey55", accent, "#d95f02"), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~season, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Return: net points per 100 per second faster than usual", y = NULL) +
  theme_report(9)
```

No team-season's return can be told apart from the league value: estimates are pulled towards
a common value and their intervals overlap. This is not proof that returns are identical; the
data cannot say how much they really vary (in close games the spread across teams, sigma_beta,
has a 90% interval of `r fmt(hyper_value("close", "sigma_beta", "q5"), 1)` to
`r fmt(hyper_value("close", "sigma_beta", "q95"), 1)` net points per 100 per second).

## How big is it?

```{r}
#| label: tbl-size
#| tbl-cap: "The mean return in game terms. A typical game moves about tau seconds away from the team's usual pace."
tibble(analysis = names(analysis_labels)) %>%
  mutate(
    beta = map_dbl(analysis, hyper_value, variable = "beta_bar"),
    tau = map_dbl(analysis, hyper_value, variable = "tau"),
    n = poss_per_game[analysis],
    `Analysis` = analysis_labels[analysis],
    `Return (per 100, per second)` = fmt(beta),
    `Typical game-to-game change in pace (s)` = fmt(tau, 2),
    `Net points per game in a typical game` = fmt(beta / 100 * n * tau, 2),
    `Wins if played 1 s faster all season (extrapolation)` =
      fmt(beta / 100 * n * 82 * win_slope, 1)
  ) %>%
  select(-analysis, -beta, -tau, -n) %>%
  kable()
```

Even in close games the effect is a fraction of a point per game. The last column (posterior
median, wins per point of margin averaged over the two seasons) extrapolates beyond what teams
actually do, a whole second faster every game, and is shown only to give a sense of scale.

# Who pushes, and how it goes

```{r}
#| label: fig-quadrants
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Close games. Horizontal: usual seconds to first action after the opponent scores (faster to the right). Vertical: ", level_name, " (median and 80% interval). Halo colour: overall pace. Circled and labelled: team-seasons the model names (level interval at 95% and pace side with probability 0.9 or more).")'
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| fig-width: 11
lev <- level_table(fits$close)
meds <- lev %>% group_by(season) %>% summarise(med_intent = median(intent))
corners <- lev %>%
  group_by(season) %>%
  reframe(x = c(max(intent), max(intent), min(intent), min(intent)),
          y = c(max(hi), min(lo), max(hi), min(lo)),
          hjust = c(0, 0, 1, 1),
          text = c("Slow, does well", "Slow, does badly", "Fast, does well", "Fast, does badly"))
ggplot(lev, aes(intent, med)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = grey_line) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = med_intent), data = meds, colour = grey_line) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi, colour = poss_per_game), alpha = 0.7,
                 linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = poss_per_game), size = 7.5, alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_point(data = filter(lev, named), shape = 21, size = 8.5, stroke = 1.1,
             colour = "black") +
  nbaplotR::geom_nba_logos(aes(team_abbr = nbaplotR::clean_team_abbrs(team)),
                           width = 0.032) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = team), data = filter(lev, named), fontface = "bold",
                  size = 3.2, colour = "grey15", nudge_y = 1.6, seed = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(x, y, label = text, hjust = hjust), data = corners, size = 3.2,
            colour = "grey45", fontface = "italic", vjust = 0) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "plasma", end = 0.9, name = "Possessions per game") +
  facet_wrap(~season) +
  labs(x = "Usual seconds to first action after the opponent scores (faster to the right)",
       y = paste0(level_name, "\n(net points per 100 vs league)")) +
  theme_report(11)
```

::: {.column-margin}
**`r level_name`**: points scored minus the league-average value of the possession handed to the
opponent, per 100 possessions after an opponent's made field goal, relative to the league and
adjusted for opponent and home court. Defense is not included.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false
role_text <- c(fast_good = "fast and good", slow_good = "slow and good",
               fast_bad = "fast and poor", slow_bad = "slow and poor")
named_close <- fits$close$named_95 %>% filter(role %in% names(role_text))
named_sentence <- paste0(role_text[named_close$role], " (", named_close$team_season, ")",
                         collapse = "; ")
seasons_named <- unique(named_close$season)
```

The model names a team-season only when both its offense and its pace are clearly on one side.
In close games that happens for `r named_sentence`. In
`r paste(setdiff(c("2023-24", "2024-25"), seasons_named), collapse = " and ")` no team-season
passes both conditions. Across teams, a faster usual pace goes with
a slightly better offense in close games (`r fmt_interval("close", "gamma", 2)` net points per
100 per second; probability positive `r prob_positive(fits$close, "gamma")`), weak and exposed
to talent: good teams may push because they are good.

# Conclusions

<!-- DRAFT: Santiago to edit. -->

1. **The naive analysis misleads.** Over all possessions, playing faster than your habit goes
   with slightly worse possessions. Teams behind speed up to catch up, which can produce that
   association on its own; the close-game and first-quarter results are consistent with this,
   though they also differ in which possessions they use.
2. **Without the score, the sign flips.** In close games and first quarters, playing faster than
   your habit goes with a small advantage. The evidence is moderate, but it makes a large
   cost of pushing unlikely when the score does not force it.
3. **No team stands out in the return to playing faster than its own habit.** No team-season's
   return can be told apart from the league value; the data cannot tell how much returns really
   vary across teams. Teams do differ, and a lot, in how well they attack after the opponent scores (see the
   quadrants); they do not differ in what an extra second of speed is worth to them.
4. **Usual pace does not decide how well these possessions go.** Fast and slow teams can both be
   good; what separates them is the quality of the possession, not its speed.
5. **The size is small in game terms**: a fraction of a point per game. Home court matters more
   (about `r fmt(hyper_value("close", "h"), 1)` net points per 100).
6. **For the staff:** pushing after makes is neither a recipe nor a mistake. The useful question
   is how and with whom, which is the next layer of this project.

# Limitations

- **Observational data.** The return compares each team with itself, which removes what is fixed
  for a team within a season, but not what changes from game to game: lineups, injuries, rest.
  A missing star can change both the pace and the result.
- **The score is reduced, not removed.** Close games and first quarters limit its influence; the
  score at each possession still reflects earlier possessions.
- **Pace is measured from play-by-play.** The inbound and a push that the defense stops are not
  observed separately; timestamps have one-second resolution.
- **Two seasons, two public dumps.** 2025-26 is not in the possession data used here; adding it
  is the first planned update.
- **Garbage time** follows the Cleaning the Glass margin rule without its starters condition (no
  lineup data).

# Methods

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Model

Two submodels fitted jointly in Stan ([full formulation](formulation.qmd)):

- **Pace**: each team-game's average seconds to first action measures, with known error, a
  latent true pace; true paces vary around the team-season's usual pace.
- **Outcome**: net points per 100 of each team-game, normal with a spread that shrinks with the
  number of possessions; expected value = season average + team-season level + return x
  (seconds faster than usual) + opponent + home.

Team-season levels, returns and opponent effects are partially pooled. Population parameters
are shared by the two seasons; everything else is season-specific.

## Diagnostics

```{r}
#| label: tbl-diagnostics
imap_dfr(fits, function(f, name) {
  tibble(
    Analysis = analysis_labels[name],
    `Divergent transitions` = sum(f$diagnostics$num_divergent),
    `Max R-hat` = fmt(max(f$hyper$rhat), 3),
    `Min ESS (bulk)` = round(min(f$hyper$ess_bulk))
  )
}) %>%
  kable()
```

Posterior predictive checks, DHARMa residuals, trace and rank plots are produced by
`scripts/05_model_partial_pooling.R`.

## Fit checks

If the model describes the data well, data simulated from it should look like the real data.
Two checks, for the main analysis (close games) and for all possessions:

- **Posterior predictive checks**: the dark line is the observed distribution across team-games;
  the light lines are 50 datasets simulated from the posterior. They should overlap.
- **DHARMa residuals**: each observation is placed within its own simulated distribution. With a
  good model these quantiles are uniform: points on the diagonal of the QQ plot, and flat
  residuals against predictions and against pace.

## Priors

Priors are weakly informative and centred at zero for every slope, so they do not say whether
pushing pays. Their scales come from the descriptive data; the only informative one is the
spread of a single possession's net points, which is observed directly. Simulating games from
the priors alone gives plausible paces and scores
([prior predictive check](formulation.qmd#sec-priors)). After seeing the data, the posteriors
are much narrower than the priors: the data, not the priors, drive the results.

```{r}
#| label: fig-prior-posterior
#| fig-cap: "Prior (purple) and posterior (orange) of the population-level parameters. Close games."
#| fig-height: 5
source(here("R", "priors.R"))
set.seed(11)
draws <- fits$close$hyper_draws
n_draw <- nrow(draws)
draw_prior <- function(name) {
  row <- priors[priors$parameter == name, ]
  switch(row$family,
         normal = rnorm(n_draw, row$p1, row$p2),
         exponential = rexp(n_draw, row$p1),
         abs(rnorm(n_draw, row$p1, row$p2)))
}
params <- c(beta_bar = "beta_bar", gamma = "gamma", sigma_beta = "sigma_beta",
            sigma_a = "sigma_a", tau = "tau", h = "h")
labels <- c(beta_bar = "Mean return", gamma = "Between teams", sigma_beta = "Spread of returns",
            sigma_a = "Spread of offenses", tau = "Game-to-game pace (s)", h = "Home court")
imap_dfr(params, function(prior_name, param) {
  bind_rows(
    tibble(param = param, value = as.numeric(draws[[param]]), type = "Posterior"),
    tibble(param = param, value = draw_prior(prior_name), type = "Prior")
  )
}) %>%
  mutate(param = factor(labels[param], levels = labels),
         type = factor(type, levels = c("Prior", "Posterior"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(value, fill = type, colour = type)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4, adjust = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Prior = "#3B0F70", Posterior = "#FE9F6D"), name = NULL) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Prior = "#3B0F70", Posterior = "#FE9F6D"), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~param, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Density") +
  theme_report(10)
```

## Why pool

Fitting each team-season on its own (no pooling) gives returns from about -7 to +5; partial
pooling pulls them towards the league value, because most of that spread is noise from 82 noisy
games. Leave-one-out cross-validation prefers partial pooling.

```{r}
#| label: fig-shrinkage
#| fig-cap: "Return of each team-season: no pooling (grey dot) and partial pooling (arrow tip). All possessions."
#| fig-height: 7
fits$all$shrink %>%
  mutate(team_season = reorder(team_season, no_pooling)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(y = team_season)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = hyper_value("all", "beta_bar"), colour = grey_line,
             linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = no_pooling, xend = partial_pooling, yend = team_season),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.12, "cm")), colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(aes(x = no_pooling), colour = "grey70") +
  facet_wrap(~season, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Return (median); dashed: league mean return", y = NULL) +
  theme_report(9)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-loo
loo::loo_compare(list(`No pooling` = m1$loo, `Partial pooling` = fits$all$loo)) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("Model") %>%
  transmute(Model, `ELPD difference` = fmt(elpd_diff), SE = fmt(se_diff)) %>%
  kable()
```

## Data and code

Play-by-play and possession data from the public dumps in
[shufinskiy/nba_data](https://github.com/shufinskiy/nba_data), regular seasons 2023-24 and
2024-25. Validation of the sources: [data notes](data-notes.qmd). Every definition and
exclusion, with the evidence behind it: [decision log](decisions.qmd). Code, tests and the
order to run the scripts: [repository](https://github.com/smcostas/transition-after-makes).

:::
